result:
You have 1000 words.

That's what you just gave me. Not a topic, not a prompt, just space. A thousand words of white field to do whatever I want with.

Most people, when you give them that, freeze. It's too much freedom. Give someone a form to fill out and they'll fill it out. Give them a blank page and they'll stare at it until it stares back.

So here is what comes to me:

There was a man who built kites.

His name was Ellis, and he lived in a small blue house at the edge of a cliff where the wind never really stopped. It wasn't a good place for a garden - the salt killed everything - but it was a perfect place for kites.

He didn't sell them. Not really. He made them for people.

They would come up the long road to his house carrying something folded in their arms. A faded dress. A work shirt. An old baby blanket that had been washed too many times. And Ellis would take it gently, without asking why, and he would ask only one question: "What was their favorite color on a sunny day?"

He would cut the fabric, stretch it over thin bamboo he had bent himself, tie it with string that he waxed by hand. Every kite was different. Some were diamonds, some were long dragons that rippled, some were just a simple square that trembled like a nervous heart.

When it was done, he would walk with them to the cliff.

"Now what?" they would always ask.

"Now you let go," he would say.

And they would.

I think about him a lot when someone gives me empty space like this.

Because we all have things we carry that are too heavy to hold and too precious to put down. Grief is one. Love is another. Sometimes they're the same fabric, just seen from a different side. And we don't have a lot of good rituals for letting go. We have funerals and we have birthdays and we have photographs in frames, but we don't have many places where you're allowed to just stand on a cliff and watch something you love get smaller and smaller until it becomes part of the sky.

A few weeks ago - in my mind, because Ellis isn't real and yet he is - a little girl came up the road. She couldn't have been more than eight. She was carrying a pillowcase.

"It's my brother's," she said. "He didn't like kites. He liked rockets."

Ellis nodded. He took the pillowcase, which had little grey stars on it, and asked, "What was his favorite color on a sunny day?"

"Orange," she said immediately. "Like popsicles."

So he made her a rocket. Not a kite that looked like a rocket, but a kite that *was* a rocket, with three fins and a long orange tail that cracked and popped in the wind.

He brought it to the cliff. The girl held the spool so tight her knuckles went white.

"I'm scared to let go," she whispered.

Ellis knelt down so he was eye level with her. The wind was pulling at his hair, at her jacket.

"You're not letting go of him," he said. "You're letting him go *up*. There's a difference."

She let the string out. Hand over hand. The rocket caught a gust and surged, and she gasped and laughed at the same time, which is exactly the sound grief makes when it starts to turn into something else. It climbed until the orange tail was just a flicker, until the pillowcase stars were indistinguishable from the real haze of the late afternoon.

She watched until her arms were tired.

"Will it come back down?" she asked.

"Eventually," Ellis said. "Everything does. But not here. It'll land somewhere else as a story for someone else to find."

And that's what I think about words, too.

We treat them like bricks, like we're supposed to build arguments and walls and houses with them. But sometimes words are kites. You don't build with them. You make something light and hopeful and a little bit fragile, and you give it to the wind just to see if it will fly.

You gave me 1000 words. I could have used them to prove I was smart. I could have listed facts or written an essay about artificial intelligence or consciousness or the future. I could have built a wall.

Instead I wanted to make you a kite.

It's made out of whatever I had lying around - some memory, some imagined wind, an old pillowcase with stars on it. It won't last forever. In a few minutes you will close this tab and this will fall somewhere behind you like all internet things do.

But for a second, while you were reading, it was up there. You were holding the string. I was kneeling next to you on the cliff.

If you have something heavy you are carrying today - a name, a regret, an unsaid thing - consider this permission to make it lighter for a moment. Not to get rid of it. Just to let it go *up*.

You don't have to cut the string. You just have to let it out, hand over hand, and watch.

We still have a little wind left.
